questions.q: A film follows a hitman through every scene and gives us his voice-over, but we're horrified by him throughout. In Murray Smith's terms, what's going on?
questions.explain: Smith separates alignment (whom we follow and access) from allegiance (whose side we take).

questions.q: What are the two components of alignment in Smith's model?
questions.explain: We follow a character in space and time, and we get access to their thoughts and feelings.

questions.q: A writer's antihero is a drug dealer. A colleague suggests making his rivals crueler and more treacherous. Which way of winning allegiance is this?
choices: Surrounding the character with worse people, as The Godfather does
questions.explain: When the world around a criminal is worse, our allegiance tilts toward him.

questions.q: Why do audiences briefly want Norman Bates's car to sink in Psycho?
choices: Because the score tells them to
Because they've been told Norman is innocent
Because they're aligned with him and caught in suspense about whether he'll be caught
Because of a save-the-cat moment earlier in the film
questions.explain: Alignment plus suspense produces a flicker of allegiance we wouldn't endorse.

questions.q: How does Smith's structure of sympathy differ from Blake Snyder's "save the cat"?
choices: Snyder's is a recipe for allegiance; Smith shows alignment and allegiance are separate dials
Smith says heroes must be likable in scene one
Snyder's model is about sound, Smith's about image
questions.explain: You can hold an audience through access or fascination without making a character likable.

questions.q: A feature writer tells a story about a parent whose child died in a hot car, following the parent's day and reporting their thoughts. In Smith's terms, what is the writer doing?
choices: Aligning readers with someone they might otherwise condemn
questions.explain: Alignment through access can shift allegiance, as in Gene Weingarten's "Fatal Distraction".

questions.q: Which word did Smith set out to replace with his three-level model?
questions.explain: He thought "identification" was too loose and split it into recognition, alignment and allegiance.

ideas: Following a character closely and siding with them morally are two separate effects a story can set against each other.
What feels like a perverse allegiance to a villain is often fascination rather than moral approval.
The vague word "identification" breaks down into recognizing a person, being attached to them, and taking their side.
You can keep an audience with a character through access to their mind alone, without making them likable.
